newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers to open formal U.S. budget negotiations.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers to open formal U.S. budget negotiations.

text.p: Nearing the end of a years-long quest, lawmakers open formal negotiations later on Thursday to craft compromise legislation designed to balance the federal budget by 2002.

A bulky group of lawmakers first convene for a largely ceremonial session. They then split into smaller teams to hammer out the details of a final budget bill in private sessions, in concert with White House officials.

Congressional leaders hope to meld House- and Senate-passed tax and spending bills into final compromise packages, and get them signed by President Clinton, before leaving town in August for a planned recess.
"The (negotiators) will come out with a package that we will be comfortable with, the American people will benefit from and the president will sign," Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott predicted.
The legislation would implement a five-year balanced budget deal that Clinton and congressional leaders have praised as a landmark of bipartisan cooperation.

There is broad consensus on the outlines of the legislation, which would cut about $140 billion from Medicare, Medicaid and other federal programmes over five years and offer a net $85 billion tax cut.
The details are the sticky part, and in an agreeement this large there are plenty of them.

The White House adamantly opposes the House Republican version of the tax plan, saying most of its benefits would flow to the rich. They warn the tax cuts could explode in later years, increasing the deficit.

"The goal that the Democrats have of delivering a tax cut to middle income Americans ... is really facing only one remaining obstacle, said House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt. "That is the Republicans' insistence that the lion's share of this tax cut go to the wealthiest Americans."
Republicans are split internally on how to design a final tax plan but are united in challenging White House charges that they are looking out mainly for the wealthy.

Republicans cite their own economic data to argue that the bulk of the tax cuts in the bill -- including a $500-per-child tax credit, new education tax breaks and a cut in the capital gains rate -- would benefit the middle class.

Another brewing issue is a Senate-passed plan to raise the federal cigarette tax by 20 cents per pack, raising about $15 billion over five years. The majority of that money would be used for children's health care.
House Republicans are reluctant to go along with the increase. Though he voted for it, Lott does not like it.
"I don't like the tobacco tax increase because it is another tax a lot of blue collar workers in my state are going to pay," the Mississippi Republican said.
Most of the $115 billion in Medicare spending cuts in the budget measure come from reducing federal payments to managed care, hospitals and other health providers.
The Senate, by unexpectedly wide margins, voted to make affluent beneficiaries pay higher Medicare premiums and gradually raise the program's eligibility age to 67 from 65.

In a shift of position, Clinton has said he might be willing to go along with some form of income test. The White House is opposed to increasing the eligibility age, worried it could increase the ranks of the uninsured.

House Republicans want political cover from the White House before embracing the income test, although they voted for a similar plan during the last session of Congress. They are skittish after taking a drubbing from Democrats on Medicare during the 1996 elections.

Other issues remain, including differing House and Senate children's health plans. While both offer states block grants to set up their own insurance programmes, govenors complain the Senate plan is too prescriptive.
The administration believes the House plan is too loose and could result in states using the money to fund programmes other than children's health.
The bills also differ in how they would restore aid to many legal immigrants set to lose benefits this summer under a new welfare bill and cuts in Medicaid for the poor.
